#ZeroDay #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
996 network switches hacked. Through a flaw nobody knew about. 🚨

What BleepingComputer reported (4 Nov):
→ CVE-2026-107441 is an out-of-bounds write in the web management interface of Zyxel GS1900 switches; no login needed
→ It affects ten GS1900 models
→ GreyNoise saw a suspected Chinese-speaking actor it calls "Kapibala" from about 17 Aug, with 996 devices compromised in 48 countries
→ Binarly found the exploit hit a separate, unpatched bug, not the one fixed in June; Zyxel confirmed it on 11 Oct
→ Firmware fixes shipped 22 Oct; Zyxel's advisory came out 3 Nov

What to do: install the latest GS1900 firmware, keep the switch web interface off the internet and user networks, and check hardened devices that were "already patched" in June.

cover.hook: In through a dev environment. Out with password hashes.
cover.sub: Chainstack says an attacker reached production via a third-party component. Customers are told to rotate node credentials.

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: Blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack disclosed an attack on 3 Nov. It says the attacker got into a development environment on 26 Oct, moved to production, and was detected and cut off on 31 Oct.

slides.label: from first access to detection
slides.note: 26 Oct to 31 Oct 2026, per Chainstack via The Hacker News

slides.title: What was reached
slides.body: A database with organization names, account holder names, member emails and password hashes. Node credentials sat on reached systems too: "We have no evidence they were read, but we are treating them as exposed."

slides.title: The bigger pattern
slides.body: The Hacker News reports the incident is assessed to be part of a large AI-powered attack campaign and overlaps with a China-linked ARTEX campaign. Chainstack did not share specifics.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Change the password, and anywhere it was reused
Expect phishing that mentions this incident

items.question: How long would a quiet attacker last in your dev environment before anyone noticed?
items.x_text:
Chainstack: an attacker got into a dev environment on 26 Oct, reached production and accessed names, emails and password hashes before being cut off on 31 Oct. Customers should rotate node credentials and API keys.

#DataBreach #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
In through a dev environment. Out with password hashes. 🔓

What Chainstack disclosed (via The Hacker News, 3 Nov):
→ An attacker reached a development environment on 26 Oct through a third-party component, then moved into production
→ The intrusion was detected and access cut on 31 Oct
→ A database with organization names, account holder names, member emails and password hashes was accessed
→ Node credentials were on reached systems: Chainstack is treating them as exposed
→ It is assessed to be part of a large AI-powered campaign that overlaps with China-linked ARTEX activity (Chainstack gave no specifics)

What to do: rotate node credentials, regenerate platform API keys, change your password (and anywhere you reused it), and watch for phishing.

You reset your password. The attacker is still logged into your AI tools. 🔑

What SpyCloud found (via Cybersecurity News, 4 Nov):
→ Two Windows infostealers, WardenStealer and Aoki, collect AI session data
→ SpyCloud reported 130,000+ unique WardenStealer infections since first seeing it on 3 Aug 2026
→ Claude Code credentials in the logs held OAuth access and refresh tokens plus auth for connected MCP servers; Codex data held an OpenAI API key
→ Aoki logs held data tied to ChatGPT, Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, GitHub Copilot and Cursor
→ This is theft from infected endpoints, not a breach of ChatGPT, Claude or Codex themselves

What to do: revoke active sessions, rotate exposed API keys and tokens, review unusual API use, and add AI credentials to every developer-laptop infostealer investigation.

cover.hook: A quarter of OpenAI's production engineers, moved to security.
cover.sub: Reuters: staff warned leaders about security lapses for years, starting before ChatGPT launched. Based on people familiar with the matter.

slides.title: What Reuters reports
slides.body: Five people familiar with the matter say employees raised concerns about OpenAI's security practices with leaders and the board before ChatGPT launched in late 2022.

slides.label: production engineers reassigned to security infrastructure in August
slides.note: Per one person familiar, describing a move by executive Thibault Sottiaux

slides.title: The gaps described
slides.body: One monorepo was reachable by anyone at OpenAI with code access; OpenAI says it doesn't hold all code or model weights. Some tooling, like research sandboxes, had no regular security reviews; OpenAI says it now does them.

slides.title: What OpenAI says
slides.body: A spokesperson said protecting its technology, data and people is "a matter of national importance". After Reuters asked for comment, OpenAI posted that it is planning its "next internal security sprint".

slides.title: Check your own AI team
items: Who can read your whole code repo?
Do research sandboxes get security reviews?
Are model weights in a separate, logged store?
Is security staffed before the next launch?

What to do: check who can read your whole repo, put sandboxes and internal tools on a review schedule, keep model weights in a separate logged store, and staff security before the next launch.

items.x_text:
Kernel breach: a compromised API key (24 Oct) led to a staff login at its logging provider, more keys and secrets in logs, then 4 GPU servers on 3 Nov and a cryptominer. Kernel: 0.28% of customers impacted.

#DataBreach #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
One leaked API key. Ten days later, four GPU servers. 🖥️

What Kernel disclosed (4 Nov):
→ 24 Oct: an unauthorized party used a compromised Kernel API key to probe for access
→ 27 Oct: the same key got them a staff login to Kernel's logging provider, whose data held a small number of API keys and customer apps' third-party secrets
→ 3 Nov: a compromised hosting-provider credential gave access to 4 GPU servers; a cryptominer started on a dev server
→ Detected 2 Nov, contained 3 Nov; Kernel says 0.28% of customers were impacted
→ Kernel believes the attackers are financially motivated and use the AI-assisted platform ARTEX as a command center

What to do: if you use Kernel, ask whether your keys or secrets were exposed and rotate them. Everywhere: use scoped API keys, keep secrets out of logs, and lock down logging and hosting accounts with strong MFA.
